nutshell: Prior mixture-of-experts (MoE) approaches to domain-generalizable person ReID add a whole separate branch network per source domain (model size grows with the number of domains) and mostly ignore domain-invariant features. META instead shares all parameters across 'experts' except domain-specific batch-norm layers, adds a global branch using Instance Normalization to capture domain-invariant features, and at test time estimates how relevant each source domain is to an unseen test sample by comparing that sample's IN statistics against each domain's BN statistics (via Frechet Inception Distance), feeding those relevance scores into a learned aggregation module trained with an episodic 'mimic unseen domain' procedure.
contributions: Domain-specific BN-only experts instead of separate branch networks per domain: all experts share the backbone weights and differ only in their batch-norm statistics, keeping model size constant regardless of how many source domains are used - directly addressing the model-size scaling problem in prior MoE methods like RaMoE.

A global branch (Global-BN followed by Global-IN, replacing BN with IN specifically in the last residual stage) trained on all source domains jointly to explicitly capture domain-invariant features, complementing the domain-specific expert branch.

A test-time relevance-estimation scheme that computes the Frechet Inception Distance between an unseen test sample's IN statistics and each source domain's BN statistics (justified by the fact that IN is mathematically the degenerate case of BN at batch size 1), fed into a small 2-layer learned aggregation module that outputs per-expert integration weights.

An episodic training procedure with a consistency loss (Eq. 11): during training, one source domain is held out per batch and the aggregation module is trained to combine the remaining K-1 experts into a feature as discriminative as the held-out domain's own dedicated expert - directly optimizing the aggregation module to mimic an unseen domain rather than only using held-out domains for model selection.
deficiencies: The paper's own ablation (Table 6) shows the global branch alone (F-global, no expert branch, no aggregation module, no FID relevance estimation at all) performs nearly identically to the full META model - e.g., 24.1 vs 24.4 mAP on MSMT17 and 76.4 vs 76.5 mAP on Market1501 - while the expert branch alone (F-exp) performs far worse (10.2 vs 24.4 mAP on MSMT17). The text reframes this as 'feasible to only leverage the global branch for faster inference,' but it also means the paper's central machinery (domain-specific experts, FID-based relevance, learned aggregation, episodic consistency loss) adds only marginal (~0.1-0.3 point) gains over the much simpler global-branch-only design when combined at test time.

The learned aggregation module itself, isolated in Table 5 ('w/o aggregation module' vs full META), contributes only 1.1-1.4 points of mAP over simply combining experts with raw (unlearned) FID weights - a modest improvement for what the method's name and framing ('adaptive Aggregation') treat as a central contribution.

Under Protocol-1 (Table 3), META is not the best method on the iLIDs target specifically - RaMoE beats it by a wide margin (90.2 vs 83.5 mAP, 85.0 vs 79.2 Rank-1) - and this is mentioned only in a single passing sentence with no investigation of why, despite META winning comfortably on every other target in the same table.

Because DukeMTMC-reID (used by essentially all prior DG-ReID work cited here) was taken down, the paper defines three new evaluation protocols of its own; while the reason is legitimate and disclosed, it means most reported comparisons rest on the authors' own re-implementations of competing methods (marked with an asterisk) rather than numbers independently published under the same protocol, making it harder to verify the comparison is apples-to-apples.
notable: The entire relevance-estimation pipeline hinges on a simple mathematical observation: Instance Normalization is literally the special case of Batch Normalization with batch size 1, so both reduce to per-channel Gaussian statistics that can be directly compared via Frechet distance without needing any learned mapping between them - a clean piece of reasoning worth remembering for other normalization-statistics-based domain-relevance tricks. Also notable: the episodic training procedure bakes a form of leave-one-domain-out cross-validation directly into the training loop itself (holding out a domain each batch to train the aggregation module to mimic it), rather than using held-out domains only for offline model selection as most other DG methods do.
